query: For high-entropy-alloy bond coats used in thermal barrier coating systems for high-temperature applications, what single intervention could improve coating durability and reliability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Severe surface deformation of high-entropy-alloy bond coats via stationary friction processing (SFP) can improve coating durability and reliability in thermal barrier coating systems for high-temperature applications.
generation.intervention: Severe surface deformation via stationary friction processing (SFP)
generation.conditions: High-temperature applications, specifically in the range of 900-1100 °C
generation.structural_mediator: Refined microstructure with increased grain boundary density and uniform elemental distribution
generation.mechanism: Formation of an intact, dense, uniformly distributed oxide scale, favored by large grain boundary density, higher surface free energy, and uniform elemental distribution
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved oxidation resistance and reduced mass gain, leading to enhanced coating durability and reliability
generation.baseline: As-cast high-entropy-alloy bond coat without SFP
generation.boundary: Temperature range of 900-1100 °C and exposure time of up to 100 hours
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between SFP parameters (e.g., rotational speed, processing time) and the resulting microstructure and oxidation resistance is not fully understood and requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the oxidation resistance of as-cast and SFP-processed high-entropy-alloy bond coats at 1000 °C for 50 hours
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SFP-processed sample shows no significant improvement in oxidation resistance compared to the as-cast sample, the hypothesis is falsified

Benafia et al. examined the influence of surface mechanical attrition treatment (SMAT) on the oxidation behavior of 316L stainless steel. The SMAT-assisted sample showed the beneficial effects on the oxidation resistance of the 316L steel at high temperatures owing to the preferential growth of chromia in the SMAT samples. Kanjer et al. reported improved high temperature oxidation resistance of pure Ti after shot peening. The increase in grain boundary density for the nanostructured sample enhanced the N2 short circuit diffusion paths, which promoted the formation of a nitrogen-rich layer that limits the diffusion of O2 into the metal. Khanna et al. studied the oxidation behavior of Cr–1Mo steel after cold rolling and reported enhanced oxidation resistance of the cold worked steel samples at high temperatures. Cr diffuses faster toward the surface owing to the increased defect concentration in the cold-worked alloy, and the higher concentration of Cr thus available leads to formation of Cr-rich oxides and reduces the oxidation kinetics.

In contrast, both the SFP samples show a highly refined stir zone, and the grain size could not be obtained from the optical images. The depth of refinement (DOR) varies from 300 to 650 μm for the SFP_400 and SFP_1800 sample, respectively. The increment in DOR with rotational speed is likely due to the thick column of plastically deformed zone during processing at higher rotation speed. The grains of processed samples below the refined zone appear to be elongated, which is caused by the effect of shearing action and corresponds to the thermomechanical affected zone (TMAZ). Figure S1 shows the temperature profile acquired during the SFP at two different rotational speeds. At 400 rpm, the average temperature was nearly ∼280 °C, while it increased up to ∼760 °C at 1800 rpm. High temperature at higher rotational speed favors the material flow through thermal softening and leads to deeper DOR.
